source: Bonde et al. (2024) The impact of specialized software on concept generation (Design 2024)
finding: Teams using matrix software (Morpheus) that forced a reduction strategy made more sub-solution combinations than hand teams, but developed them less.
numbers: 8 teams (26 people: 17 Chalmers MSc, 9 Darmstadt PhD), coffee-maker task, 2 to 3 h. 5 software teams, 3 traditional. Every software team made more combinations than every traditional team (software 3 to 64; traditional 1 to 2 in legible rows). Mean functions in matrix 18.8 (software) vs 14.7 (traditional). Concretization n: software as low as 0.17, traditional up to 0.71.
limits: N=8 teams; authors state significance could not be reached; novelty and variety could not be scored.
agent_relevance: Enumerating combinations is cheap, but value is lost unless each is developed. Code should enumerate; the model should develop only a pruned few.

source: Bonde et al. (2024) design space size
finding: Student matrices make huge design spaces, so full enumeration is impossible and a pruning rule is needed.
numbers: Unconstrained design spaces: 6,144 (smallest listed larger team), 2.5e12 (24 functions), 5.5e12 (23 functions), 3.6e13 (31 functions). Teams used pragmatic or thematic reduction; two traditional teams left strategy undocumented.
limits: Small sample; strategy labels partly inferred. Three strategies taught: full combinatorial, pragmatic (rank functions, trim options on low-rank ones), thematic (only combinations following a stated theme).
agent_relevance: S3 open mode needs an explicit pruning rule fixed before enumeration. Pruning should be coded, not left to the model.

source: Bonde et al. (2024) behaviour of traditional teams
finding: Traditional teams settled on one or two combinations and usually did not say why; software teams were forced to state which options to drop.
numbers: Traditional teams: 1 to 2 combinations, more concrete (team G2 n=0.71). Software teams less concrete but documented their strategy.
limits: Qualitative reading by first author only.
agent_relevance: A code-required field for why a branch was cut mirrors G2/G3: record the reason, do not trust a silent choice.

source: Bonde et al. (2024) questionnaire
finding: Users found the software easy to learn; they did not feel it made concepts more innovative.
numbers: 24 of 26 answered (96%). Experience: 7 novice, 13 intermediate, 3 advanced, 1 unsure. Non-software teams were slightly more positive about having produced many innovative concepts.
limits: Self-report; no significance.
agent_relevance: Felt creativity and measured output can diverge; never accept the agent's own claim of novelty (G8).

source: Martinsson Bonde et al. (2022) Morpheus: development and evaluation (NordDesign)
finding: First version of the matrix software was used by about 500 first-year students in nearly 100 projects; it made tracking many solutions easy but students outputted auto-generated word strings.
numbers: 12 of 36 groups answered the questionnaire. Most matrices had 4 to 6 subfunctions; a majority of groups generated more than 31 solutions; only half attached images. All said easy to learn; a majority said it did not help find new solutions. Focus group of 7 teachers.
limits: Single institution, first-year students, 33% response.
agent_relevance: Failure mode to guard: combinations left as word lists. Add a code gate: a combination counts only after a written description and a test.

source: Martinsson Bonde et al. (2022) misuse as screening
finding: Students used the matrix as a strict down-selection filter against the requirement list instead of a way to synthesise concepts.
numbers: Teachers saw groups call the method a screening method in reports; some used subfunctions that differed from their functional analysis; some groups did make more iterations because edits were easy.
limits: Teacher observation; no counts.
agent_relevance: Keep generation (S3) and screening (S7) separate states, as the schema does.

source: Saurabh et al. (2022) Idea generation mechanisms: classification, combination, building on others, stimulation (J Mech Des)
finding: Four experiments isolated the combination mechanism (the core of morphological analysis) from classification. Combination helped, but classification did as well or better.
numbers: Exp1 N=61 grad students (alternate uses); Exp2 N=57 freshman engineers (garbage picker concepts); Exp3 N=35; Exp4 N=41. Exp1 unique ideas in round 2: classify about 3.7 vs combine about 1.8 (p=0.000); novelty of all ideas higher for classify (p=0.014), no difference on unique ideas (p=0.907).
limits: Short sessions, student samples, mechanism isolated from the full method, non-parametric tests, round-1 baselines not always matched.
agent_relevance: Combination alone is not the best divergence driver. Partitioning into exclusive branches first (classification) gave more unique ideas; do a coded partition, then fill cells.

source: Saurabh et al. (2022) Exp2 engineering concepts, originality
finding: In engineering concepts both mechanisms raised originality within group, but there was no difference between groups.
numbers: Mean originality round 1 to 2: control 2.33 to 2.93 (p=0.406); combine 1.57 to 2.65 (p=0.023); classify 1.89 to 3.22 (p=0.000). Round 2 between groups: Kruskal-Wallis p=0.445. Round-1 quantity differed between groups (p=0.000), so quantity was compared only within groups.
limits: Within-person pre/post design; originality via DTOAD scale (7.5 or 10 = radically different).
agent_relevance: Gain is within person; 'matrix beats free generation' is unproven here.

source: Saurabh et al. (2022) cost of the mechanism on quantity
finding: Stopping to build combinations lowered raw quantity in round 2, while radically different concepts rose in all groups.
numbers: Quantity fell round 1 to 2 for control (p=0.039), combine (p=0.003), classify (p=0.000). Combine group had the largest percentage rise in radically different concepts.
limits: Authors say effect on quantity needs more study.
agent_relevance: Matrix building costs tokens on structure; G7 says count that cost.

source: Saurabh et al. (2022) building on others vs stimulation
finding: Seeing others' ideas raised novelty and originality at least as much as structured stimuli.
numbers: Exp3 quantity: BoO p=0.182, stimulation p=0.475 (n.s.). Novelty vs control: BoO p=0.001, stimulation p=0.005; BoO vs stimulation p=0.606. Exp4 originality: BoO beat stimulation (p=0.018).
limits: Not morphological analysis itself.
agent_relevance: Supports mixing retrieved outside material with matrix cells.

source: Kirjavainen and Holtta-Otto catalogue, as reported in Saurabh et al. (2022)
finding: All ideation methods are built from 25 mechanisms; combination appears in 38% of studied methods.
numbers: 25 mechanisms; combination in 38% of methods, classification in 11%.
limits: Second-hand through Saurabh.
agent_relevance: Suggests matrix effects are mostly the combination mechanism.

source: Field (2011) Fluency and flexibility of concepts from personalised ideation techniques (ICED11)
finding: Of 244 students free to use any technique in an exam, only 44 used a systematic one; morphology users got slightly fewer and less varied options than non-users.
numbers: N=244, jet-engine split-pin problem. 23 drew a morphology table, 21 a classification chart, 200 neither. Fluency /8: morphology 3.58, classification 4.48, none 3.90. Flexibility /5: morphology 2.54, classification 3.09, none 2.88. Morphology vs none n.s. (fluency p<0.29, flexibility p<0.15); classification vs morphology fluency p<0.04, flexibility p<0.08.
limits: Self-selected technique use (not randomised); exam time limit; technique author is paper author.
agent_relevance: No morphology advantage in a field setting. Matrix quality depends on choosing good aspects.

source: Field (2011) choice of aspects, ability and course score
finding: A matrix with weak aspects narrows the space: a 3x3 table (9 options) scored flexibility 3/5, a 7x7x5 table (245 options) scored 4/5.
numbers: Fluency and flexibility correlated r=0.64 (p<0.01). Mental cutting test (N=138): classification users averaged 5.9/10, morphology users 4.3/10. Classification users scored 5% higher than morphology users on the course (p<0.02). Fluency vs visualisation r=0.04.
limits: Correlational; spatial test for 138 only.
agent_relevance: The first decomposition (S2) caps what the matrix can give.

source: Daly, Seifert, McKilligan, Gonzalez (2016) Comparing ideation techniques for beginning designers (J Mech Des)
finding: In a 102-student comparison, morphological analysis gave more elaborated concepts than brainstorming, but not more concepts or diversity.
numbers: N=102 first-year engineers, 25-minute individual session; design heuristics vs morphological analysis vs individual brainstorming. Brainstorming gave the most concepts. Creativity near scale midpoint for all. Elaboration significantly higher for heuristics and morphological analysis; practicality significantly higher only for heuristics. Controlling for quantity, no diversity difference.
limits: Only the abstract (via Crossref) was read; per-group means not extracted. Short session, novices.
agent_relevance: Cleanest controlled test found. Matrix helps depth, not breadth. Do not claim it raises novelty.

source: Sharbafi (2021) Assessment of ideation effectiveness: impact of morphological analysis (LearnXDesign)
finding: Junior design students on a 1000-floor elevator, with morphological analysis introduced after phase 1, improved on novelty, quality, quantity and variety.
numbers: Two phases, no concurrent control; four measures. Sample size and numbers not obtained (PDF blocked).
limits: Abstract page only; order and warm-up effects are confounded with the method.
agent_relevance: Weak evidence: a second phase tends to improve anyway (controls in Saurabh also rose).

source: Chen, Tsang, Jing, Sun (2024) An LLM-augmented morphological analysis approach for conceptual design (DRS 2024)
finding: Splits matrix work into decomposition, generation and combination with LLM help at each, plus a feedback loop; authors report better design quality and lower cognitive load.
numbers: No numbers or sample size available from the page I could read (PDF returned 403).
limits: Abstract only; effect sizes unknown.
agent_relevance: Closest LLM-plus-matrix study found. Its three stages match S2 (decompose), S3 (fill), code (combine). Full text needed.

source: Feng, Helie, Panchal (2025) Enhancing design concept diversity: multi-persona prompting for LLMs (Design Science)
finding: Parallel prompts, each with a different professional persona, gave more diverse concepts than one no-persona prompt; updating a set with a new persona did not reliably raise diversity.
numbers: GPT-4o, Gemini-1.5 flash, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct; five personas, five problems. H3a: 25 no-persona concepts vs 5 per persona in parallel; each concept summarised to 5 terms (125 terms); parallel scored higher diversity for each LLM. Update step: only Gemini-1.5 flash gained clearly. Sequential persona diversity steady, mean about 0.52 to 0.55 (SD about 0.02).
limits: Not a morphological study; diversity is spread of LLM-extracted terms, not human-rated novelty. Only partial read of results.
agent_relevance: Parallel isolated attempts, each with a different slot value, raise spread; fits matrix rows filled in independent calls (S3).

source: Jiang and Luo (2024) AutoTRIZ (ASME IDETC)
finding: A neighbouring structured-ideation method run by an LLM. Repeated runs scatter, and 7 of 10 textbook cases matched or half-matched the expert in the top 3.
numbers: 10 textbook cases, 100 repeated runs each; entropy scale 0 to 6.64; cases 5 to 8 were consistent.
limits: Not morphological analysis. Textbook expert is not a gold standard.
agent_relevance: The same structured method run repeatedly diverges, so selection of cell values needs code-held sampling (G4).

source: Ritchey (2002, rev. 2013) General Morphological Analysis
finding: General morphological analysis (Zwicky lineage) adds cross-consistency assessment: compare every pair of values once and delete configurations holding a contradictory pair.
numbers: Example field 2,304 configurations (4x4x4x3x3x4); the original 10-parameter shelter field had over 500,000. A field of 100,000 configurations needs only a few hundred pairwise checks. Author has directed over 100 projects since 1995.
limits: Proponent source; no controlled comparison; no outcome data against alternatives.
agent_relevance: Cross-consistency is a pairwise check code can run, with each pair a small model slot. It prunes the space before any scoring.

source: Ritchey (2013) scope and limits of GMA
finding: Method is meant for problems that cannot be modelled in numbers; it gives no causal or quantitative prediction.
numbers: No effect sizes reported.
limits: Proponent only; anecdotal project count.
agent_relevance: Use for open design questions, not for tasks with a checkable answer.

source: Bonde et al. (2024) gap statement
finding: Authors know of no earlier integrated software framework for matrix strategies and say their study could not reach significance.
numbers: Three workshops, 8 teams.
limits: Stated by authors.
agent_relevance: No large replication of morphological analysis effects was found in the sources opened. Treat effects as weak.

source: Zwicky (1969) Discovery, Invention, Research through the Morphological Approach
finding: Founding text; jet-engine morphological box said to reveal hundreds of unconsidered configurations (second-hand via Bonde 2024).
numbers: Not checked here.
limits: Not opened; second-hand.
agent_relevance: Read first-hand before using any number.

source: Shah, Kulkarni, Vargas-Hernandez (2000) Evaluation of idea generation methods (J Mech Des)
finding: Defines the four effectiveness metrics (quantity, quality, novelty, variety) later matrix studies use.
numbers: Not read; cited in Bonde 2024.
limits: Second-hand.
agent_relevance: Use the four metrics to evaluate S3.

source: Olvander, Lunden, Gavel (2009) Computerized optimization of the morphological matrix (CAD)
finding: Optimisation over matrix cells for aircraft concepts; Bonde 2024 says it needs per-cell models, and Pahl and Beitz warn early-phase optimisation is weak.
numbers: Not read.
limits: Second-hand.
agent_relevance: Scoring cells by model only helps with a real evaluator (G8).

source: Search coverage note
finding: Rate limits blocked Semantic Scholar, OpenAlex, the arXiv API and several PDFs; no replication, meta-analysis, or other LLM-plus-matrix study with numbers was found beyond the lines above.
numbers: Web search budget was exhausted after 3 calls.
limits: Gaps: numbers for Chen 2024 and Sharbafi 2021, Daly 2016 per-group means, a patent-based LLM matrix paper (LDA and NuNER) seen by title only.
agent_relevance: Rerun later for numbers.
